utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and to those listening to our procedures. Before the next witness will be brought in, we have to deal with one problem related to a document. This is the transcript of the testimony of this witness in the Krstic case. This is still under seal. We raised this problem last Thursday and I take it that the Prosecution is moving for lifting the confidentiality. If this is my -- the correct understanding, perhaps you can help me, Mr. McCloskey, then we have to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We will move that. That will obviously make my summary easier. I can refer to his testifying and as well as the whole process and it fits with everything we are trying to do and this witness' desires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is the witness aware of the fact that the previous testimony in the Krstic case will no longer be under seal but that the confidentiality will be listed? Does the witness know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we've spoken and basically told him that with his new view of things, that now everything would likely become public and that I'm not sure I gave him the details of where we were in that, but I am confident he understands that it's all a public now and he is fine with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, Mr. Gajic, you have indicated last week that the Defence has no problem with lifting the confidentiality of this exhibit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, you are right. We support the motion. Actually, the Prosecutor pre-empted us with the request to lift the protective measures. Even before the Prosecution proposed that, we had already prepared a motion for the lifting of the confidentiality from the Krstic transcript to be lifted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Further to the Chamber's oral ruling of the 10th of September this year, in light of both parties' submissions, the Chamber orders that the confidentiality of Rave's prior testimony in the Krstic case will be lifted pursuant to Rule 75 (G)(ii). The witness should be brought in now. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe we've estimated an hour and a half for this witness, and I hope to take much less than that, though I have made my summary a little bit longer than I sometimes normally do, but I hope to be much less than an hour and so I hope we are not going that far, but my outline suggests that to me right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When you mentioned the time of one hour, you are not referring to your summary but to the examination-in-chief, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, sir, Mr. Rave. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown it to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You know unlike your prior testimony in another case, you are now testifying in open session without protective measures. We have heard from the Prosecution that you gave your consent with this variation of the previous protective measures. You are in agreement with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey will have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you fist tell us your name and spell your last?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: My name is Evert Albert Rave. And Rave is R-a-v-e.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you recall testify in the Prosecution versus General Krstic back in March of 2000?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was that testimony true and correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, they would exactly be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to review your transcript in that case?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, and it's still the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we all notice that you are speaking in English. You are Dutch by nationality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was it your choice to speak in English?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes. I did it in the Krstic case exactly the same, I think, and shouldn't be a problem to do it again in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at this time, Mr. President, I would offer P01004 which is the transcript from the Krstic case into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As well as the material noted that came in through him in that case, P01005, a video still; P01006, another video still of Lieutenant-Colonel Svetozar Kosoric. It may be PO as I'm looking at this. PO 1107. Sorry, I'm told it is a zero. P01007 is the video still of Colonel Radoslav Jankovic. And then we have the segment P00991 of the Srebrenica trial video, and the transcript of the Srebrenica trial video is P01008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These documents will be received but I have to note that P991 is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And the Court will remember seeing the video in other formats before. All right. Now, I will read a summary of your testimony before and then ask you a few questions. In 1995, Evert Rave was a warrant officer 2nd class with the Dutch army. And he was a member of the Dutch Battalion deployed to the Srebrenica enclave on 3 January 1995. His rank was that of sergeant-major. In July, 1995, Mr. Rave was assigned to the Dutch Battalion base in Potocari and held the position of a liaison officer and advisor of field security for the commander of the Dutch Battalion, Colonel Karremans. As liaison officer, Mr. Rave had regular contacts with the civilian and military people from the Muslim community inside the enclave and various officers of the VRS located outside the enclave. As field security officer, Mr. Rave advised the commander on protective measures relating to personnel, materiel, information, and other military issues. As liaison officer for DutchBat, Mr. Rave had contact with the commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic, Major Momir Nikolic from the Bratunac Brigade, a VRS interpreter known to him as "Petar" and others. Major Nikolic was Mr. Rave's principal contact for issues related to the enclave and the VRS. On 31 May, Mr. Rave was at a meeting with Major Nikolic and a VRS officer named Vukovic where the VRS officers told DutchBat that DutchBat would have to leave OP-Echo or the VRS would take it by force. On 3 June, the VRS attacked OP-Echo and the DutchBat soldiers stationed there withdrew from the OP. On 6 July, the VRS began attacking the enclave, targeting UN OPs during the attack. The attack continued through 11 July. During that time, VRS shells fell near the UN compound in Potocari and the UN compound in Srebrenica. The OPs were targeted causing Dutch soldiers inside the OPs to surrender to the Serb forces to avoid being targeted by Muslim soldiers who were angered by the Dutch withdrawal from the OPs. At times, Muslim soldiers would fire at the VRS forces from around the area of the OPs in order to draw VRS fire on the OPs. In Mr. Rave's view, this was done by the Muslim forces in an effort to get the UN to fire on the VRS. According to Mr. Rave, the enclave was never fully demilitarised. On 9 July, the UNMOs had to leave Srebrenica because it was no longer safe there. Also on 9 July, the roughly 4.000 Muslims living at the Swedish Shelter Project south of Srebrenica began fleeing to the town of Srebrenica. On 10 July in the evening, DutchBat commander Colonel Karremans and Mr. Rave met with civilian and military representatives of the Muslim population in Srebrenica. At that meeting Colonel Karremans told the Muslims that air-strikes would occur on the VRS forces if the VRS attacks continued the next day. Mr. Rave spent the night in the Srebrenica UN compound, known as "Bravo Company." On the morning of 11 July, the VRS attack continued and shells fell in and around Srebrenica town, including inside Bravo compound, wounding several people. At 3.00 p.m., Major Boering, a DutchBat officer, and Mr. Rave left Srebrenica to Potocari in a jeep crowded with Muslim refugees. On the way to Potocari, shells fell along the road and Rave felt the VRS were using their fire in an attempt to move the crowd in the direction of Potocari. On that day there were brief air-strikes but they had no significant effect on the assault and did not last long. At 5.00 p.m., Rave returned to the Potocari base and estimated about 10- to 15.000 frightened Muslims were in the area around the UN base. At 7.00 p.m., Colonel Karremans ordered Rave to go to a meeting with Karremans and Major Boering, the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac. Rave arrived at the Hotel Fontana at 8.00 p.m. with Colonel Karremans and Major Boering. Upon entering the hotel, Mr. Rave saw several UN soldiers who had left their OPs and surrendered to the VRS. In addition, Rave identified the following people present and inside the hold: General Mladic, General Zivanovic, Colonel Jankovic, an officer introduced to him as Kosoric, and Major Nikolic and Petar, the interpreter. Mr. Rave testified that he remembered that General Mladic personally yelled at both he and Major Boering, just as can be seen he did to Colonel Karremans on a video of that meeting. However, Mr. Rave stated that the tape did not contain the segments where Mladic yelled at him and Boering. Mr. Rave also testified that General Mladic told them if there were more air-strikes, Mladic would shell the UN compound and the refugees gathered in Potocari and would also target the UN soldiers held at the Hotel Fontana. These comments by Mladic were also not on the film segment that Rave watched. At that time, Mr. Rave felt that it was possible that he, Karremans, and Boering would be taken outside and shot. General Mladic told Karremans to find a Muslim representative and bring him back to the hotel at 11.00 p.m., among other things at the meeting. Rave testified they went back to Potocari where they were able to find Nesib Mandzic, who they knew as a teacher from the secondary school in Srebrenica and brought him to the Hotel Fontana at 11.00 p.m. as a civilian representative. At the second meeting where they were taken in and sat down, Mr. Rave was unable to follow much of what Mladic was saying because Petar was translating for Colonel Karremans, and Rave was unable to hear the complete translation because Colonel Karremans and Petar were seated away from him. Mr. Rave described a pig being slaughtered just outside the meeting room window and he felt this was done to intimidate DutchBat and Mr. Mandzic. Mr. Rave testified and described the continuing meeting as sometimes, and I quote, "rather relaxed," and other times, and I quote, "very mean" on Mladic's part. On 12 July, Mr. Rave spent the morning at the compound in Potocari. Rave described the VRS entering the compound at Potocari area and the frightened reactions of the Muslim population. Rave witnessed the separation of Muslim men from their families and the boarding of men on buses. He described that he saw men hit and kicked on to the bus at one point when they tried to get away. On the morning of 13th July, Mr. Rave received a report that DutchBat soldiers found nine Muslim bodies near the compound, who had been shot in the back. Photos were taken of the bodies by DutchBat. Mr. Rave saw Colonel Jankovic in and around the Potocari on both the 12th and 13th of July. On 13 July, a VRS officer named Acamovic arrived in Potocari and took part in organising the transport of the Muslims. Acamovic was provided a list of local Muslims employed by DutchBat and other international organisations in Srebrenica, such as MSF. That list was provided to him by DutchBat. By 8.00 p.m. on 13 July, the Muslim population of the enclave had been transported out of the enclave. On 21 July, DutchBat and local staff left the enclave and travelled to Zagreb. That concludes the summary of the Krstic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Rave, was there anything inaccurate that you recall in the summary?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, I think it's a correct summary from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I notice you have a binder in front of you and I can see there's some coloured books in there. Can you tell us what that material is?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I brought my notebooks which I used during all the meeting we had and with the Muslims and with the Serb soldiers we dealed with, which I took my notes just when former commander or just to analyse what was going on or just reminders for myself. And I brought my diary in which I wrote every evening small part what happened that day and more or less my own feelings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review that material as well as the different statements you made prior to your testimony back in 2000 in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I had the possibility and I also did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And have you had a chance to review that material again before testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, the same answer, I had the possibility and I also did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, all that material has been provided to the Defence. Some of it for quite a long time, others of which we had expanded the area of the diary a bit and it's all been translated into B/C/S and provided with the Defence also. It's not my intension to make it exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But Mr. Rave, if you need to refer to that to help refresh your recollection, I don't think that will be any problem, but if you could let us know what you are referring to to do that so that we understand what that is. All right? Okay. You testified that, I believe it was on 11 July, a shell fell in the Srebrenica compound injuring some people. Can you tell us what people did you mean in the Krstic transcript?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: On that morning, a lot of civilian people from Srebrenica were gathered outside of the compound and would not be allowed to go into the compound. At one time there were so many people and they broke through the fences and went on the compound because they were looking for a safe place to stay. In their point of view, the UN compound was safe for them to go there. So a lot of Muslim, especially women and children, were gathered on the compound of the Bravo Company and also elderly men, and at a certain time a mortar shell, I think at least it was a mortar shell, it was a shell, landed between two APCs on the compound, luckily between two APCs so only a few people were wounded by that shell, so civilian Muslim people were wounded by that shell and after that treated by the medical personnel that was on the Bravo compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you actually see the shell land or see the impact of the shell as it landed or sometime afterward?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Just sometime afterward because I was not on the spot at that moment. I heard that a shell landed and directly after that we were confronted with the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say you heard that the shell landed, did you hear that from word of mouth that a shell had landed or did you actually hear the sound of the shell?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I heard the blast of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how far away was that impact from you when you went out to see it?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think between 25 and 50 metres because the parking-lot of the compound was just beside the buildings and we were in or just outside the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You also testified explaining how you were trying to get the Muslims to go in the direction of Potocari. Why did you and the DutchBat do that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: There were so many people gathered on and around the compound of the Bravo Company that we could not do anything with the people. The VRS attack still continued, and in our opinion it was the best and the safest place to go northwards to the bigger compound in Potocari. So we tried to inform the people that it was better for them to go to Potocari, but there was of course a problem. They had the idea that they were in a safe haven at that moment and they didn't want to go there until, I think, 2.00 in the afternoon. There were some air-strikes at that moment, the people got a little bit trust that something was done to the VRS in the southern part of the enclave, and don't know why, but at that moment we were able to send them northward to the Potocari area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You described your ride in that jeep, the 5 kilometres to Potocari, you described shells falling around. Can you describe that for the Court, how -- where these shells were falling, how far away they were from you as you were travelling?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: The road from Srebrenica to Potocari is in a valley, and in my impression all the time shells were falling between the 150 and more metres on both sides of the road. And I had the idea that it was just to keep the people on the road and to move them in the northern direction so that the VRS could get all Srebrenica in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the road, clearly you are on the road, is anybody else on the road?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: The refugees from Srebrenica went up to the northern part to Potocari and I think that the road was overcrowded with thousands of people walking with all their luggage with them. Some UN vehicles from the Bravo Company, especially trucks with also the wounded from the hospital in Srebrenica were on the road, so the road was also overcrowded, and driving on that road was just going step by step in a vehicle over that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of shells were falling? Were they mortar shells, artillery shells?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, in my opinion, but I have to recollect it now, and it's 15 years ago, I think it were mortar shell. But I also did not write it down in my diary, just that there were shells falling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any potential target for those shells, any Muslim Army or any other target for these shells to be falling on either side of the road as you have described, as this massive group of people is walking along?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, there were no military targets. In my impression it was the only opportunity to steer people from Srebrenica in the northern direction towards Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We are now getting to -- I want to take you to the first meeting at the Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, you may remember, it was a long time ago, we actually played this meeting with no witnesses, I believe we had a video day where we just played it. I would like to play part of it today so Mr. Rave can add a few details, but I don't intend to play all of it. So if we could start with that video. It's Exhibit P00991, and we are starting at 003649.9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before we start the video, we recall from the summary, have you had a chance to review the video that we showed you of that first meeting?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that a complete video of everything that you recall happening at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, as you stated before, I missed some parts of the things that happened over there, especially the part that when General Mladic shouting to Colonel Karremans. After that he did the same to us, me and Mr. Boering, well this, at least not on the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's, I would like to play the video and see if we can tell what you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again we are at 36.56.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just -- let's go from left to right, and I think we all recognise General Mladic on the far left. Were you introduced to the person next to him?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the Colonel Jankovic. And after that, to the right in the middle, you can see the Colonel Karremans and then myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so you are on the far right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you ever seen Colonel Jankovic before that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, I've never seen him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see him at the second Hotel Fontana meeting that night at 11.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, he was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see him in and around Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Jankovic was all the time around even to the last day as we left the enclave near Yellow Bridge -- near the iron bridge in Bratunac he was also there, so from that moment on we saw him the first time until we left the enclave he was frequently there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- well, as we see is there any translation going on here or attempting to go on?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I missed the video now, but at that moment there was no interpreter. Colonel Jankovic spoke English and acted at that moment as a translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did that change at some point?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, before the real interrogation or accusation by Mladic started, the interpreter Petar came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think let's -- let's just watch this for awhile and I'll just have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no video at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we are okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Here it appears we see Colonel Karremans saying he is not the one that requested the air support. Was that true?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think he requested the air support, fired in the normal chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are stopping at 50.22.6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We did see awhile back General Mladic had raised his voice quite a bit. Is that what you were talking about when you say he raised his voice at General Mladic -- excuse me, at Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, he seemed to be very angry at Colonel Karremans because of the loss of his soldiers in the attacks by the aeroplanes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't see as this tape continues any screaming at you or Boering. Can you recall where that happened in this sequence of events?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, I think in my opinion it was also directly after the screaming to Colonel Karremans that he also started screaming to me and to Mr. Boering, so this, at least, part I'm missing in this tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the threat as you described against the -- well, why don't you in your own words tell us what the threat was that he made against who?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: The way he acted now against Colonel Karremans, he did the same to Mr. Boering and to myself. The way he was looking, the way he was shouting, the way he was acting, the way it was translated by the interpreter was so threatening to us that I, in the first ten minutes I think, and that's what I wrote down in my diary, the first ten minutes I thought we will end up in the garden and he will shoot us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What particular threats did he make?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: During the whole meeting, he gave us the impression that he is the boss, we had shot at his soldiers so he would do the same to us, that's the impression he gave us. And somewhere in the meeting, I think it is a little bit further on, he gave the impression that if there should be any air-strikes again, that he would target the compound, the refugees and also the soldiers that were held hostage or POW in the Hotel Fontana at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I don't think the tape shows any of those direct threats towards the UN compound, the refugees, or the Dutch soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, I have not seen that on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know in this sequence at the Hotel Fontana when he made those threats?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: In my opinion, it was also in the beginning of the meeting when he was shouting and when he was threatening us because after those threats it became a little more calm, and, well, at least at that moment, we could hear the demands of General Mladic because there was no negotiation going on, it was just hearing his demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Unless the Court want to hear the rest of it, we have our witness presents, I'm satisfied that the transcript is there, and, of course, General Tolimir can play more on cross if he'd like. But I think to save some time, I don't think we need to play the rest of it, unless you'd like to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we are in agreement with your proposal. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just a clarification: Did I understand to mean that this meeting was requested by General Karremans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, that might be possible. The only thing I know that at about 7.00 in the evening I got the order to join Colonel Karremans to the meeting in the Hotel Fontana. And I don't know if it was on the request of General Mladic or the Serb side, or it was on the request of the Colonel Karremans. As it seems now on the tape, it stated that it was on the request of Colonel Karremans. That might be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have a question. Mr. McCloskey, you say that you are not going to continue playing the video. Does this mean that today we are not going to see the passage where there's the pig, the pig that was slaughtered? Is this what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What I meant by that is that this is still the first Hotel Fontana meeting as we call it, and I thought that it wasn't necessary to show any more of that. I have been going back and forth in my head whether I should show the pig, and I think we can show that pig part briefly and ask this witness about it. So I think, especially given your question, it's probably a good idea to show that part and ask him about it. That's at the second meeting and we'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we'll come back to this because I believe that it is very important for me, and you also mentioned this in the summary of the statement that you read earlier, so I would like to come back to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. That helps me decide that point which I've been going back and forth in my head. These 92 ter witnesses, we try to give you what we think is most important and that helps me quite a bit. All right. We'll let that be in the record. The transcript and the video is something the Court should have, as you know we are endeavouring to let you have good CDs of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we know from the summary that you were told to -- by Mladic to go get civilian and military representatives and bring them back for an 11.00 meeting. And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes. At that moment I think we told already General Mladic that it was very problematic for us to get in touch with the military leadership in the enclave because we had no contact at that moment with them. So we informed them already at that moment, but we were able to find a civilian representative that we met before in the enclave and who was willing to join us to the 11.00 meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: It was director of the secondary school in Srebrenica, Mr. Nesib Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what do you recall about the beginning of that meeting and the pig?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: In that meeting we came into the room again, sat down. At that moment, I don't know if the window and the curtains were already open or were opened at that moment, but the window at least was open and after that the meeting started. I think the meeting, from my notes, the meeting started 11.00, and five minutes later, I had the impression that beneath the window that was opened and the curtains were open, that a pig was slaughtered outside just to intimidate the people inside the briefing room where we were sitting, and, of course, not the Serb side because at least lieutenant, and seemed to be Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric, started smiling and also other people were grincing [phoen] when the pig were slaughtered, at least when we heard him scream, and when it hardly ended they closed the window and closed the curtains again, so at least the meeting started with an intimidation towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you said people were smiling and grinning?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Grincing I had the impression that it was all arranged in advance and people knew what was happening or was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe what window you are talking about, where it was in relation to where you were sitting and where General Mladic was sitting?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: It was the window behind General Mladic and to the right side of myself. Most right corner of the window when you entered the room, the main entrance and then you look towards the window, and on the most right side there was a window that was opened and also the curtains were opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you said you had the impression that a pig was being slaughtered. Was that only an impression or what did you mean by when you said you had the impression?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Well, I wrote also down in my diary that a pig was slaughtered. Of course I did not see that it was slaughtered so it can also be treated very bad, but I think that it was slaughtered, at least I have heard that scream from a pig before when it's slaughtered and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, tell us about that. When, if ever, had you ever experienced the slaughtering of a pig?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: My grandfather was a farmer and I've seen slaughtering of a pig over there, so I recognised, at least, that sound and that's the sound I related to the sound I heard that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You also just said something about a pig makes a noise if you treat it very badly. Can you tell us having had some farming experience what is the difference, in your view, between a pig being slaughtered and a pig being, you know, held up by it's legs or something like that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, when you keep a pig with his legs or on his tail or on his ears, then it starts screaming and stops when you stop. And in this case, I had the impression that it faded away slowly, so maybe his throat was cut or something like that. Because that's the impression I still have and what I find in my diary that the pig was slaughtered, so I made at that time directly the connection that the pig was slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you read -- can you go to your diary, if that is all right, and just read specifically what you say about that? You've mentioned that several times. And before you read it, can you tell us when you wrote the notes in this diary?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: These notes were written down during the meeting, so when we started the meeting, I started to wrote down the meeting I saw in the meeting. We started it was three people DutchBat, on the 11th of July at 2300 hours. The people who were there. And then the first note I made 2305 pig slaughtering on film, sound, window, curtain open, smile, men with cigar pipe and moustache and tank, I know now that was Lieutenant Kosoric, I refer to in this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What does the tank have to do with Colonel Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: In my recollection, he has the tattoo of a tank on his arm -- yeah, tattoo on a tank -- tank tattoo on his arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you read out your notes in English. Are they in English or in Dutch?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, they are in Dutch. I can read them in Dutch, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why don't you do that just for the record, in case it's an issue. It's all right. We hear a lot of Dutch around. It's only a few words so if you could just say it.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: [Dutch spoken] [In English] That is on Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll get a translation of that for the record, Mr. President. I don't normally like doing that, but I just, as I'm concentrating through this, I thought that was a good thing to get down so it's been so interested by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's, of course, not on the record, but it was taped and perhaps we have the chance to get a proper translation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that, just seemed like something we should get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I have no further questions, so I turn you over to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I thank Judge Nyambe for letting me put my questions first. Witness, as you probably know, I went to Sarajevo and I also went to Hotel Fontana, I saw the briefing room. Now, this is my question: Are you sure that the pig was slaughtered in the street or was he slaughtered -- or was this pig slaughtered in the kitchen of the hotel? That's my first question. Okay. You gave us your impression of the situation. I thank you for that. You told us what your impression was when it comes to the slaughtering of the pig, but this is what I would like to know, I'd like to know whether after the fact you actually discussed with the Muslims to see what they felt about what had occurred and whether you discussed also this incident with the Serbs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think you are asking me three questions now. I think that the kitchen of the Hotel Fontana, in my opinion, was not at the outside of the window where the window was open and the curtains were open. I think that's somewhere outside the hotel and I don't know exactly if the window has a view on the street or in a garden or something else, but at least not in a kitchen. It just happened and I think we might have spoken about it afterwards, but not at that moment during the session we had in the briefing room over there, and I also don't think that we spoke with the Serbs afterwards about the incident. It was just one of the things that happened, and, well, it was just one of the intimidating things. That's it and I think we had a lot of more important problems to solve than this at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I did mean to play that segment which may be helpful for any future questions so that we can see the area and get an idea what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that would be helpful, but before that Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, like Judge Mindua before me I've had the opportunity to visit Hotel Fontana and being in the actual meeting room that you referred to. My question is: Having stated yourself that you are a farmer and you've dealt with pigs, and you are familiar with what happens to pigs when they were being slaughtered, what is it about the slaughter of this pig that you perceive as an intimidation towards you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think first I have to take away a little mistake, I think. I'm not a farmer, my grandfather was farmer and there I heard and saw the slaughtering of a pig. And because I knew the sound of the slaughtering of a pig and heard that sound the same evening we were in the Hotel Fontana, that's why I made the connection of a slaughtering of a pig. Because when you slaughter a pig, it starts screaming and yelling in a terrible way, at least for normal people, I think. In my opinion, it gave the impression: What we can do to the pig, we can also do to the Muslims. That's what the impression what I got at that moment. It was pure intimidating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of any special or significance of a pig or a pork in the Islamic religion?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course in the Islamic religion it's not allowed to eat pork or -- and normally they also don't have pigs, although in the enclave we were, there were also Muslims who had pigs and who slaughtered pigs. Sometime when we had no fuel anymore, we had to close down our cooling facilities, we had a lot of pork meat and also a lot of other meat, we asked the Muslim leadership in the enclave if it was allowed for us to give the pork meat to the Muslims in the enclave. They refused because they said it doesn't fit into our religion. So we don't accept it. So we gave it to the Serbs to deal with both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know if you considered this the religious tradition when you were thinking whether -- this issue about intimidation or not?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, I don't think I connected it to a religious thing. Just more intimidation of slaughtering, in this case a pig, but it also could have been a dog or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's play the segment. And we are at 01.16.10.0. And this is the beginning of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now we are at 01.16.23.1. We can see Colonel Jankovic and we can see the left hand, do you know who that is sitting next to Colonel Jankovic who we can't quite see, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, was sitting there, that's Petar the interpreter next to Jankovic, then the Colonel Karremans and then Nesib Mandzic. And the guy who is standing over there is the man who I frequently saw near the General Mladic and I think he was a body-guard of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know who is sitting next to Jankovic who we can't see, all we can see his left hand?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Left to Jankovic is General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell from this video where the window might be that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: The man who is standing over there is standing in the open, I don't know if it's open, standing there near the window. I think it's open at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And could you tell where the sound of the pig was coming from?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: From the direction the man is looking toward now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's play the rest of it and see if there's any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We are now at 01.18.22.8. And I think we'll all agree for several seconds before this we heard a very loud screeching sound. Was that what you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, that's, in my opinion, the slaughtering of the pig.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you said that Kosoric was smiling. Where was Kosoric sitting when you noticed him smiling?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: He was sitting opposite me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So opposite across the table from you?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was he smiling before that terrible noise?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, he was just making note of -- taking notes. And when this happened, he started smiling and grincing in a way, so nice trick isn't it, that's the way he looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We all noticed Colonel Karremans didn't look up, didn't appear to make -- have any reaction at all. Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, I think it's amazing that he doesn't react at all. I think he is so into his own mind, busy with in dealing things, that he want to bring across the table to the General Mladic that I don't even know if he recognised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Later on in this video we see General Mladic speaking to Mr. Mandzic and says something to the effect that, Nesib, the future of your people is in your hands, whether they survive or disappear. Have you seen this on this video?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen that part of the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember it happening in the room or was that something that you couldn't catch the translation of because, as you've described, the translator was not right there?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: In my notes, I can't find it. I can read in my notes that about 2315 he shows us a shield from the opstina, tells a story, and then makes a show about that he found nothing in the hospital, medicines, and after that he had a real, in my opinion, a relaxed discussion with Mr. Mandzic. After that Mladic gave a statement it was about 20 minutes after 11.00, and directly after the statement of Mladic -- statement of Mandzic, Mr. Mladic gave a statement towards Mandzic again and he was accusing him and had a mean look in his eyes that it was all their fault, and I think in that part he also told that the future of his people were in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that the end of your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, do you have cross-examination with this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I would like to welcome the witness. May God's peace reign in this courthouse and may his will be done and not necessarily mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let's start with the scene that we saw last, with the last video-clip that we saw and what you said on page 27 of today's transcript from line 10 onwards, when you spoke about your feelings and impressions. Kindly listen and see the video-clip again. You say that you heard a pig. Could you please try and reflect whether you heard -- whether that was indeed a pig or some sort of poultry. Thank you. After that, we will continue our conversation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecutor please play that part of the video-clip if the witness wants to listen to it again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Ms. Stewart will endeavour to find that spot where it starts. And maybe I can, just for the record, state where it starts. We are starting at --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The sound starts at 01.17.30, thank you, on the video. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, this is not correct. This is 01.17.00.8.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you mentioned your grandfather having been a farmer, would you say that this is the screeching of a pig or of some other animal?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: In my opinion, this is the screaming of a pig.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you sure of that, of what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Of course I'm sure. And that in my opinion, this is the screaming of a pig. If any other animal that is slaughtered makes the same noise, that could be possible of course. But in my opinion, this is a slaughtering of a pig. And that's what I think now, but that's what I also felt in the evening we were sitting there and that's what I also find in my notes so that's the only recollection I've got.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since nobody reacted, Karremans didn't, Mladic didn't, Petar the interpreter didn't react, how do you account for that, how come nobody reacted to the sound?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think I can only give my impression and what I think. Because if you want to know why they don't react, I think you should ask them. As I said, I think it was all preset. It was arranged in advance and maybe before we entered the room, as DutchBat representatives, the rest of the people might have been already informed that this was happen. In my opinion, it's amazing for me to see that Colonel Karremans does not react at all, and I think he might be so intense with his notes and with the way he brings it up to the General Mladic that that might be the reason that he doesn't react. But I don't know, I think you should ask Colonel Karremans in showing him this why he doesn't react.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me whether there were any people who did not know and they didn't react? Karremans didn't react, and we can see on your face that you didn't react either. We can replay the video again. Mandzic, for example, he didn't react either.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I didn't see on the video during the slaughtering of the pig the face of Mandzic or myself because I was not sitting next to Mandzic. There was another person sitting next to Mandzic. I did not see myself and I did not see any other reactions and only the face of Petar and Colonel Karremans. Maybe we can try the video again and see if there's anybody else not reacting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And before we ask the Prosecutor to play the video again, would you say that Muslims would be intimidated by the slaughtering of the pigs if they, themselves, were eating pigs? You said it yourself that there were Muslims who kept pigs and ate pigs. It was not uncustomary in Bosnia for Muslims to eat pigs. There were those who were religious and didn't eat pig, and on the other hands there were those who did. So once again were there Muslims in Bosnia who did keep pigs and who also ate pigs?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I know that in the enclave there were Muslims that kept pigs and were eating pigs. But the intimidation, I think, is very clear. After having been in a real war situation for several days, being shelled for several days, more than 15.000 people running and fleeing because they are threatened to death, I think, gathered around the compounds with no idea what is going on, what is happening with them, then especially Mr. Mandzic picked up as a representative from the refugees going with us to meeting where we did not know what to expect again after the first meeting, we only got a lot of orders from the General Mladic what he wanted. After that, we went there with a frightened civilian with us who was not allowed to go out of the enclave for several years, was going out now for the first time to the Serb side, did not know what he could expect. So he was frightened already, and I think at that moment slaughtering a pig beneath the window, it was enough intimidating and not only normal slaughtering of a pig that happened when people want to eat the pigs they raise themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether the scared civilian was a soldier, and do you know that that person ventured as far as 15 kilometres into the Serbian territory and killed every person to the last in Kravica? Do you know that or perhaps not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That kind of vulgar misstatement and accusation is uncalled for. It should not be allowed on the record and I would ask that General Tolimir never repeats such vulgarities again. Unless he has evidence, if he has proof of something, he can say -- or evidence of something he can put that in a question, but there's no evidence of any murders by Mr. Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you want to know something from this witness, you should rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a witness stated before this Trial Chamber that he was in Kravica. Another witness stated that everything was torched and everybody killed there. If this is not proof, what is proof? I can't bring you people who were killed and that's why I asked him that, that's why I said what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, this is not true, Mr. Tolimir. You were directly referring to Mr. Mandzic in two sections. Please rephrase your question and then put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that Mr. Mandzic participated in sabotage and assault actions during which Serbian villages were torched and Serbian population killed together with everybody else who was in those villages? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should rephrase your question. You have heard the objection of Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard the objection, but I don't know what you want from me. The witness said that that person was scared, that he never left the enclave. I'm asking him whether he knows that he actually did participate in fightings and that he participated in sabotage actions. I hope you can allow me to put that question to the witness. If not, then that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, may I ask you, do you know anything about Mr. Mandzic participation in combat activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the only thing from Mr. Mandzic I know that he was a teacher before the war, and he was a teacher during the war. And I have no information that Mr. Mandzic played a role as a soldier or anything else and went out of the enclave to do whatever is suggested. So I have no information about that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Rave, you are not a protected witness, I may as well call you by your name. Mr. Rave, could you please tell us whether your impressions and your feelings, and so on and so forth, is something that you shared with any of the participants in that meeting that had been called on Karremans' request that evening in order to discuss the evacuation of the Muslims from the enclave?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Do you want to know if we later on discussed the information we got on that meeting? Yes, of course, after we came back to the compound we had a meeting and we discussed what was said during the meeting and what were the first important steps we had to deal with, and that was put on paper by Colonel Karremans, and on that we acted further. I think that he sent the information also in his chain of command upwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And did you discuss the intimidation with anybody on the Serb side, the intimidation that you have just described for us?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, because after we -- it was not discussed during the meeting and not directly after the meeting. That were the only moments we were in contact with the Serbs, and for us this was just one of the incidents that at that moment happened and we had to deal with more important things because we had 15- or 20.000 refugees without any food, water, or sanitary things. So it was just an incident that happened at that moment and we had to deal with more important things than only slaughtering of a pig.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it's the right time for our first break of today's hearing. We will adjourn and resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, would you please tell us, had you been to Fontana Hotel before these events, before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I've been there several times before. The first time was in the, I think the 6th of January, 1995 when we had our hand-over meeting with the previous battalion, and we also did it in Hotel Fontana over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to observe if this Fontana Hotel had an economic section, some courtyards, something like that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, the only thing I've seen from the hotel that when we were brought there most of the time we were accompanied by one of the soldiers who brought us over there was that we entered in the hotel, were brought to one of the briefing rooms and because I think there were more and I can't recollect especially, but I think there were more briefing rooms. And we were seated in the briefing room, and the first meeting we had over there they preferred -- they prepared the food for us and all the time they were serving drinks and small food, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that on that footage the body-guard of General Mladic stood by the open window? My question is: Would he have observed or seen or heard something going on outside the hotel and would he have maybe opened the window to see if there was some threat to the person he was guarding? Why would he have opened that window?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: As I said, in my opinion it was all pre-arranged. I don't know if he opened the window by himself or that he got a sign from somebody to open the window at that moment. The same for closing the window. I don't know if he decided it for himself when to close the window or that he got a sign that he could close the window at that moment. At that moment I have not seen him before afterwards I seen him several times accompanying General Mladic and I've not seen that he took decisions by himself, only when he was ordered by the general or just doing the normal protective thing, normal protective measures for the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were in charge of security in the field, would you able to tell us whether a body-guard in war time can take any security measure without the approval of the person he is guarding?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I'm not a specialist in body-guard measures, but I think that a body-guard is always able to take protective measures, also in war time because there are, of course, lots of threats he has to be aware of, and I think that they should be trained in protecting the man who he is in charge for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us if the Fontana Hotel, which you had visited in January and at other times, was privately owned and did it operate normally under the circumstances because it was not directly on the front line?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I have no idea if the hotel was really in use as a hotel because I only visited for the meetings we had with the Serbs over there. I know that one of our logistic NCOs went there to trade with the owner of the hotel, and I think it was the owner because that's what the my opinion was told all the time for buying some beer or refreshments to use for us inside the enclave because we had nothing and we had the possibility and were able to go to the Hotel Fontana and deal over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show to the witness D37.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's a document dated 10 July 1995. The title is "Approval to slaughter and distribute livestock."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this will be appear on the screen, I have a question for the witness. Sir, Mr. Rave, could you perhaps -- are you able to recall, I am not referring to this document, I'm still dealing with the video of the Hotel Fontana meeting. Do you recall what the body-guard at the window did later? Was he remaining at this position or what did he do? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the only thing I can tell you is that on the video I see that he is walking behind Colonel Karremans and so I don't think that he was standing at the window, but I can't recall what he did and even if he stayed in the room or might have gone outside. In my opinion, he was one of the guys who stayed all time in the briefing room, but not on the place where he was -- when the window was opened, but near the door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You just said that you saw on the video that he was leaving his position at the window behind Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I saw somebody walking. In my opinion it was the body-guard who was walking from the window back to the door where I think he stayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At which point in time did that happen, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly then. We should see the video again, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine for the moment. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, please, Mr. Rave, could you look at this document, the English version is on the left, and see that it's a document from the Drina Corps command dated 10 July 1995, that's the day before the event. They did not know that Colonel Karremans would be asking to meet Mladic in the hotel, and it says: "To be sent to the Bratunac army-operated farm, Captain Mirko Blagojevic. So they sent this permission to slaughter and distribute livestock." And it says, paragraph 2: "It is hereby approved that for the purposes of the UN soldiers billeted in the hotel in Bratunac, you may slaughter and deliver one hog up to 80 kilos." From this we see that UN soldiers who were billeted, were staying at the hotel in Bratunac and they were ordering certain foodstuffs that they needed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: This is very interesting. As I told you, and you might know, that the soldiers that were in the Hotel Fontana, were, in my opinion, hostages or POWs as you might call them during that time because I think there was a war going on at that time. I have not the impression that the soldiers were free to do what they wanted, and of course they could demands for a pig or whatever they wanted, but I think that there was only one person who granted their demands and that was Colonel Mladic. I think they were not -- well, they might be billeted in the hotel, but not as we see it now as billeted in the hotel, and also myself, free to go and free to order what I want. So I don't think that the soldiers were able to order a pig for a barbecue or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you don't seem to believe me, I'll read this whole thing once again: "It is hereby approved that for the purposes of the UN soldiers staying in the hotel in Bratunac, you may slaughter and deliver the following: One hog weighing up to 80 kilos. The hog shall be delivered through the hotel in Bratunac on orders from the commander of the Drina Corps. In selecting the livestock for slaughter, make sure that these animals are not suitable for fattening and breeding." And this is dated a whole day before that meeting. Now, could this assistant commander for logistics who signed this have known that Colonel Karremans would be asking to meet General Mladic in the Fontana Hotel precisely on the 18th [as interpreted] when you came there for the second time.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: As I told you before, I don't know who arranged the meeting. I don't know if Colonel Karremans asked for the meeting or if General Mladic or somebody else asked for the meeting. And of course, I also can't tell you what happened before we had a meeting over there. So I don't know who filled out this form, where it was sent to and I've never seen it before, so I have no idea about the logistics at that moment in and around the Hotel Fontana because the 10th we were not there, and the 10th I think I was in Srebrenica myself. And we didn't even know that on the 10th in the evening we had to go there. At least I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It may be a translation issue, but it says he went there on the 18th. Just alert that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Said 11th, not 18th, and here in the telegram it says the telegram was sent on the 10th of July at 1210 hours, and it was transmitted at 1300 hours. My question is: The owner of the hotel or General Mladic, could they have known a day before at 12.00 or 1.00 p.m. that Colonel Karremans would be asking for a meeting at the hotel the next day?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, I won't be rude but I can't get in the mind of the hotel owner or General Mladic on the 10th of July. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see from this document that a whole day of preparation is needed to slaughter a pig and that an order is necessary from the person who issues approvals normally to distribute animals to the UN, for instance?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the internal logistic lines of communication within the VRS or within the town of Bratunac, so, well, if it's stated over here and it takes that time, well, it will be so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were UNPROFOR soldiers in the Bratunac hotel, soldiers to whom this document refers, people who ordered a pig to be slaughtered?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: When we came in the meeting at 8.00, the soldiers from our OPs in the southern part of the enclave were brought to Bratunac were assembled in one of the briefing rooms in the hotel. Mr. Boering went in with Colonel Karremans and myself and visited in advance of the meeting the soldiers just for a short time. After the 8.00 meeting, we had all the possibility to go into that room, shake hands with the guys. I do not know if they were living in the hotel or somewhere else, but they were in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether it's obvious from this document that the slaughtering of one hog weighing up to 80 kilos was approved for them?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Again, I don't know the logistic rules of the VRS at that time. And I think that a young pig and a hog is ordered over there, that doesn't say anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the Fontana Hotel, were there any other UN soldiers apart from Dutch men, and did you see Dutch men in the Hotel Fontana, Dutch soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: The only Dutch soldiers that were in the hotel were our people who were made POW on the OPs on the southern part of the enclave, and the three of us who were attending the meeting, so Mr. Karremans, Mr. Boering and myself. That were the only people that I know that were there. So no United Nations military service or anybody else, only the people from the battalion including the three I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long had the soldiers been in the Fontana Hotel before that meeting?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't know how long they were in the Fontana Hotel. I didn't ask it myself to them. I know and I should look into my notes when the OPs were taking over by the Serbs and when they surrendered to the Serbs and after that were taken to the Hotel Fontana. I think it was on the 10th of July that they moved forward because they were not able to go backwards because they were stopped by the Bosnia -- the BiH soldiers over there, so they had to go forward then were captured and then were brought to Bratunac, and I don't know if they directly were brought to the hotel or were somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show P994 to the witness in e-court. Page 5, paragraph 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see paragraph 5, and I will now quote from your statement written in July 1995 just after the events: "We arrived at the Hotel Fontana about 2000 hours. As we entered, we noticed that in a separate room, some Dutch soldiers who had been manning the OPs were held under guard by the VRS soldiers. We were initially not permitted to see them. The hostages appeared relaxed and in no immediate danger. I understand that Major Boering did, in fact, manage to get access to them for a few minutes before the meeting started." Now, my question is: Did members of your delegation in the Hotel Fontana, like Major Boering, see the hostages? Did they really look relaxed and did they tell you that they had voluntarily moved to the territory controlled by the VRS because the Muslims did not let them cross their territory and one soldier was even killed while attempting to do so, and because also they were asked to shoot at members of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think you've got a lot of questions at this moment. And I think I will answer them and try to answer them one by one. Major Boering, when we entered the hotel, just bluffed and went into the room where our soldiers were, so they got -- he got access to them for a few minutes before the meeting. So, yes he saw the hostages. And what he told them and what I later on saw that they looked rather relaxed because they really didn't know what was going on. They voluntarily moved forward, and I think then Mr. Tolimir is mixing up some things, that one of the soldiers was killed, this has nothing to do with going forward from the other OPs. When the OPs in the south were attacked by the VRS, they tried to do their normal military job, that means as the General will know, going backwards, finding a new position to do your job, maybe to shoot at your attackers. The Bosnian army was there, was standing behind our APCs and was not allowing them going backwards to do their job in the way they learned and then they should do the job. The Bosnians -- the Muslims had only one idea, your enemy is in front of you so you have to go forward and if you go backward, we'll shoot you in one way or another. So there was only one way for the manning on the OPs, that was going forward and surrender to the VRS. So that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Trial Chamber, if you know, who killed one of your soldiers during your withdrawal through the Muslim territory to the base in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: When they returned from the OP, and I don't know exactly, I should look in my notes from which OP returned, a lot of people on a dirt road tried to stop the APC because they had the same intention, they had to go forward. At that moment, the commander of the APC took the decision to drive through something, people, I think, put on the road. At that moment, and I still don't know either there was a hand-grenade thrown or there was a shot from a gun that hit one of our soldiers and later on the day he died. But that was a civilian population near the OP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if those civilians were Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: The civilians were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were those civilians armed or not?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Well, as I say, that they either --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Give a pause.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- shoot or threw a hand-grenade and that implicates in my opinion that they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did DutchBat soldiers who were at the Fontana Hotel complain in any way of anything that was provided to them at the hotel, either food or something else? Did they complain to those who were in contact with them, those from the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: At the moment we spoke to them, that was on the end of the 8.00 meeting, I got no complaints from them. They only wanted to know what was going on and when they were able to return to the battalion. Afterwards, I have not spoken to them what happened in the hotel and if they had any complaints. I even don't know exactly when they returned to the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your answer you just said that they didn't know anything and they were relaxed. They didn't know what was going on. A relaxed person, would you say that that person is relaxed because he doesn't know what is going on or whether he is just confused?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think that they didn't know what was going on, they were in a situation that they were hostages or POWs and just were waiting what was going on, then you can do -- can do several things. You can get very nervous and do all strange kind of things, but you can also be relaxed and hope that the problems will be solved, and when you see your battalion commander passing by, then I think you get some hope and hope that your problems will be solved, because, in my opinion, it's the most important thing for them, their security and their return to the battalion to go back to their own jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Those soldiers or those prisoners or hostages as you call them, had they voluntarily surrendered to the VRS? Could they have done it to the Muslim army or could they have returned to their base across the Muslim-held territory?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, as I stated before, they were not able to do their military job in a way they are trained to do their job because they were threatened by the Muslim Army to go forward and fight to the VRS. So they voluntarily surrendered to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please answer the following question: Prisoners of war and hostages, are they allowed to order anything from the hotel restaurant, for example, a pig weighing 80 kilos, as we have seen in the document?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Of course I can write in a document whatever I want when I'm in a situation that I'm a hostage or a POW. I can ask, of course, as much as I want and I will ask as much as I can, but if it is allowed and you get your demands, depends on the hostage-takers, so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers about this issue. We'll come back to that issue later. On page 823, lines 13 through 18 of the Krstic case transcript, you were asked by the Prosecution to describe the peacekeeping mission. You answered, and I quote: "We were supposed to protect people within the enclave. We were supposed to provide assistance to NGOs, Medecins Sans Frontieres, the NHCR, and we're also supposed to assist them with the supplies of food and other things in the enclave for the civilian population. We had men at observation posts and we possibly also could avert attacks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, this is P1004. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question based on what I've just quoted is this: The role of the Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica, was it based on what you described or was it rather the demilitarisation of the area?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think it was both. We had to demilitarise the Bosnian army, the Muslim army in the enclave, and further on protect as much as possible and help as much as possible the civilian population and the NGOs in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Dutch Battalion demilitarise the population in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
