utterances.text: We demilitarised as much as possible in the enclave, and that already started some years before when the Canadian army was in the enclave, they started to collect the weapons and demilitarise the enclave, that went on with the first and the second Dutch Battalion in the enclave. We collected lots of weapons. We took care that there were no military activities in the enclave. And, of course, at the end we discovered that although we did our utmost to especially disarm most of the people, we did not completely succeed in disarming them all because there still remained a lot of weapons hidden in the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce D20. This is a report based on the debriefing about Srebrenica. Page 12, paragraph 22 and 23. Thank you. I apologise, it is not page 12, but page 10. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This report says: "The Dutch Battalion has been provided with the aforementioned tasks which were based on the agreement on cease-fire. Firstly, to monitor compliance with the cease-fire. Secondly, to disarm the BiH army. Thirdly, to assist with the delivery of humanitarian aid." And then in paragraph 2.30 which we are going to see in a minute --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be displayed, 2.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where you can see it serves as the last paragraph on the page, it says: "The mission of DutchBat. The military task was to maintain the status quo. As a result of the UN presence, the VRS was to be deterred from launching an offensive on the enclave and the BiH was to respect the demilitarised status of the enclaves. Several heavy weapons and a large number of hand-held weapons surrendered by BiH personnel were held in the weapon collection point controlled by DutchBat, located at the compounds in Srebrenica." Thank you, end of quote. My question, based on what I've just read, in practice was one of the tasks of the DutchBat to disarm the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could the General tell the witness and, well, for the rest of us, what report this is? There's many, many, reports. If we could have the first page just so we know which one you are talking about. That's all. And if you have a list of cross documents, Ms. Stewart would gladly accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was going to request the same so that we know who wrote the report and the date of the report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is D20, and I said that it is a report based on a debriefing about Srebrenica. Page 10, paragraph 223, and this report was published in Assen on the 4th of October, 1995, and now you can see the title page of the debriefing. We can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll repeat the question for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In practice, was one of the tasks of the Dutch Battalions to demilitarise Srebrenica, rather to disarm the BiH army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, it was one of the tasks. And as I said, it started with the Canadian company who was there, and after that, the first and the second Dutch Battalion we went on with trying to demilitarise the whole enclave by collecting as much weapons as we saw. We were in a rather good contact with the civilians and the military leaders in the enclave, and we spoke to them several times and that people were not allowed to carry weapons that they were ordered to deliver the weapons to the patrols or to DutchBat. And the other way, all the time we saw people armed in the enclave we tried to disarm them, collect the weapons and store them in the weapon collection points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In paragraph 27, you say -- and the mike is on, I believe, yes. You saw in paragraph 27, can you please show it to the witness, 27 to 30, where it says, you can see it now, where it says that the BiH Army was supposed to honour the demilitarised status of the enclave. My question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the record, Mr. Tolimir, are you referring to 2.27 or to another paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Paragraph 27, 2.30 which we see in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In front of us we have 2.27.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. 2.30 is what we need. I misspoke when I said 27. 2.30. I apologise, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says here that the BiH army was supposed to honour the demilitarised status of the enclave. You can see it in line 4. It says: "The demilitarised status of the enclave." Thank you. My question based on this, could you explain to us the meaning of these words: Demilitarised status of the enclave, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: That at that moment the status was demilitarised. At least I think that's what you want to hear. And that that status should be respected. Well, I think that that status was not -- not reached yet and so we went on with the demilitarisation of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During the DutchBat mandate, did any of the weaponry that you had taken from BiH army members arrive in your weapon collection point, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, it happened several times that weaponry that was taken not from BiH army members, but from people in the enclave, and I don't know if it were army members, but it were armed people in the enclave, the weapons were taken and storaged in the weapon collection site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you whether you know if the number of barrels of 300 at the beginning was increased by a single barrel during mandate of the Dutch Battalion? That's what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact number of barrels in the weapon collection point, the only thing I can tell you that is that during the DutchBat III period, and that's what I'm talking, not over the DutchBat I or II periods, but in the DutchBat III period, I know for sure that we took several weapon from people inside the enclave and stored them in the weapon collection point. I don't know the exact numbers that were there when we got into the enclave, and I don't know the exact number of weapons that were there at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Muslims were being armed with additional weapons in the enclave? And you already answered those questions during the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you have already received an answer, you should move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did move on to a different topic and I asked the witness whether he knows that Muslims were additionally armed in the enclave and how were they armed. He only touched upon that subject in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can give you an answer again, I don't have any information that Muslims were additionally armed during the period that DutchBat III was in charge over there, so that weapons came into the enclave. We have no information that that they additionally got armed again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, could you tell us if you heard from your predecessors or was it conveyed to you if the Muslims in the enclave were being additionally armed and if so, how was that done, which routes were used to additionally arm Muslims with weaponry?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I have also no information from the previous battalions that they were additionally armed in one way or another. So the only information I can give you is that we all as the first and the second in the Serb battalion did the utmost to disarm people in the enclave and to take care that all the weapons were stored in the weapon collection points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Muslims being armed from helicopters from Zepa to Tuzla, or rather from Tuzla to Zepa and then a land route which was taken to transport those weapons from Zepa to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: As I stated before, I have no information that Muslims having been armed during the period that we were there in charge of neither by foot, neither by donkeys, neither by helicopters, neither by fixed aeroplanes. In no way or another I've got information that they got armed additionally.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown D67. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at the document, sir. The Trial Chamber already knows it, Prosecution knows it, so I won't be reading it, I'm just going to have questions for you once you have looked at the document. And I particularly ask you to look at bullet point 2, as well as bullet point 4, starting with the words: "Preparations for future operations to merge the enclaves for brigade commanders and the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division." Thank you. Were you able to look at the two bullet points that I asked you to look at?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, but I would like to start on the top. I don't know when this should have happened, it's a report from the 13th of July. I don't know what period we are talking about. When we could go back to the first page it's a document stated -- the date is 13th of July, 1500 hours. I don't know about which period that we are talking about 17 helicopter flights are carried out. Is that on the 13th of July, is that before? I don't see any dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You were wondering who drafted the document. The document was drafted by the BiH army. It was dispatched on the 13th of July, 1995, as you can see at the top, and it was sent to the Brigadier-General Hajrulahovic to be forwarded to the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. And you will see later that the document was signed by Rasim Delic. And in this document, he informs the president of the Presidency as to what he had done in order to strengthen Srebrenica in military terms. I quoted from bullet point 4 where it explains in the last sentence why the division commander did not come back. The division commander who was meant to go on the next helicopter flight did not return. After the final flight ended tragically, Naser stayed behind. My question is this: Do you know if Naser was in Srebrenica during the time of the events about which you are testifying in this courtroom? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think that I can state that Naser was in the enclave, and I have to look in my notes until when. I think until March or April when we could negotiate with him. After that he disappeared. Nobody will tell us where he was and I have not seen Naser after March/April in the enclave anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this report then relate to the time during which you also were in the enclave? It says that the helicopters were flying and Naser did not come back because the penultimate helicopter had been brought down. And it all happened in the year 1995.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: As I can state, I don't know if Naser was in a helicopter that was brought down. I only know that I didn't see Naser after March/April any more. Maybe I can say that there was a rumour that the second in command from the BiH army in the enclave was told that he went down with a helicopter. I don't know exactly where because that was a topic that could not be discussed with the BiH because nobody would tell us something about it and we had no information that there was a really helicopter crashed or helicopters came into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you know that before the VRS attack started in order to demilitarise Srebrenica, that the Muslims launched attacks from the enclave in the depth of the Serbian-held territory?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: There were a lot of rumours, especially coming from Major Nikolic when we dealed with him as liaison officers, that he was telling us that people were going in and out the enclave and doing attacks on Serbian targets. We have never been able to prove it. We were also not able to patrol and to check the whole enclave. The biggest problem from us was that I think in February we got our convoy with fuel, so from that time on it got less and less and we were not able to patrol with vehicles, just only go around by foot. So we were not able to do our job very properly, and all the time we asked Mr. Nikolic that if he was complaining that Muslims were going out of the enclave, we told him that he had to allow fuel to get into the enclave so we could do our job properly. He had never shown us the proof that Muslims went out of the enclave, so it was for us no more than a rumour. And, of course, when we got the information that in a specific area, the VRS told us that Muslims were going out of the area, we tried to patrol over there as much as possible. But we have never been able to prove that Muslims went out of the area to attack VRS targets. And, of course, if we had known it, we would have taken actions to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see P994 page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, for the sake of the record, you were referring to the earlier to a part of the Krstic transcript. This is on page 44 -- 45, sorry. You said on page 823, lines 13 through 18 of the Krstic case, transcript, but the testimony of this witness starts only at page 830. So for the sake of the record it would be helpful if you can provide us with the correct quotation. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It could be a mistake. I should have said 832 instead of 823.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court kindly show P994, page 3, paragraph 5. That's the last paragraph we see here on the screen from your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say: "The 31st May meeting was held at Observation Post Echo. The Serbian side was represented by Colonel Vukovic and Major Nikolic. Captain Melchers and myself attended from the Dutch Battalion side. At the meeting Colonel Vukovic made several main points concerning activities inside the enclave. First, he explained that Muslims were leaving the enclave and were killing Serbs as they were leaving. He said that the situation was deteriorating around the location of OP-Echo, as the Muslims were attacking Serbian positions through the timber factory in river Jadar. As a result of this, he said the Serbian troops needed to move in to occupy the area around the observation point." Now, my question: At this meeting in May, did the VRS announce to you that Muslims were making incursions from the enclave into Republika Srpska, that they were killing Serbs and that because of that an intervention was needed to prevent it?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I have my notebook over here, and in that meeting I think that it was Colonel Vukovic, because I think he did the speaking at that moment, told us that five men were killed and two were killed short time ago. He told us that, as stated also in my statement over there, that they went through the factory to the wood factory, and that he would not attack but that he had positions in the southern part of south of the enclave. It's the same as what Major Nikolic told us several times, that BiH soldiers or civilians don't know at least Muslims from the enclave went out of the enclave and killed people outside. In this case, he directly told us that people were going out via the wood factory in the southern part near OP-Echo and I don't know if you know the situation over there, but I think that the factory and the observation post I think there might be 100, 150 metres between, so if it was possible for the Muslims to go through the factory, then I think that most the time, of course, people from the OP-Echo had seen it and had stopped him. I don't know -- of course this is a statement of the Colonel Vukovic and I can't imagine why he is telling us this and why he has concrete to the point telling us that they are going through the factory, because I think it all fits in the plan that they already had made. So the point of view from which you are looking at it, for me it's just one of the statements from the VRS that Muslims are going out of the enclave, one side. We should protect the Serbs by keeping the Muslims inside the enclave. The VRS is taking all the measures to that care that we can't do our job properly and we are not able and were not provided with the things we needed to build new OPs to do our jobs mobile, by vehicles, because we had no fuel. So it's a circle that is going around and around, and the only thing I can see also in this one is that we are making a lot of excuses why things are going wrong. And at the same time I think that we find a lot of possibilities to show what is wrong and to create a situation that they have to attack us because we are not able to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if all that is preplanned and designed, as you say, is it also predesigned that these Serbs were to be killed in the territory under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't know if it's preplanned. I only know that there were lots of rumours in that Muslims went out of the enclave to kill Serbs. Outside the enclave I have seen some results from attacks inside the enclave where people were killed that we found, the one that was guilty for that. I only know that the feeling at the moment I was in that meeting, that was that Colonel Vukovic was looking for possibilities to show us that we did not want to do our job properly, and he told us that he needed the road south of the OP-Echo, we had to withdraw and if he would stay on the OP-Echo, we had to take the consequences. And also, and that he stated in advance in one of the previous meetings that of course we showed him that also VRS people came into the enclave to kill Muslims. At that moment he told us, Well, you are free to kill every BSA soldier or every Serb [sic] man in the enclave. In the meeting of the 31st, he told us that he can no longer stay, to his point of view, that all BSA men in the enclave may be killed. So it's a game from one part to the other and, yeah ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, I did not stop you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see D53 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's a document of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated 17th June, 1995. It was written by the General Staff of the ABH, and it was sent to the command of the 28th Division of their land forces that were in Srebrenica. It's called: "Preparation for offensive combat operations. Order." You can see it now. It was signed by Sulejman Budakovic. It's not Vukovic. In fact, you will see whether Vukovic had any influence on the writing of this. It says: "Pursuant to a verbal order issued by the commander of the General Staff of the BH army, Army General Rasim Delic, and on the occasion of the great success achieved by units of the BH army in the wide area around Sarajevo and Gorazde, as well as on the basis of intelligence that the Serbian army command of the protection regiment in Han Pijesak is holding parts of its units in reserve so that they can intervene in case we attack from Zepa, I here by issue the following order:" Now, I'm reading paragraph 1: "Execute all preparations in the command of the 28th Land Army Division to execute offensive combat operations." Paragraph 2: "Plan realistic tasks which will assure certain success on the basis of an accurate assessment, and the potential of our forces in Srebrenica and Zepa." And 3: "The General Staff of the BH Army will regulate, by an order to follow, the commencement of offensive combat activities in the zone of responsibility of the 28th Army Division." And it was signed by Brigadier Sulejman Budakovic. Now, my question is: Is this a preparatory order written based on offensive operations by the VRS or based on offensives by the BH Army against the VRS and certain attacks originating from the enclave in which they had certain success?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think in my opinion this is just a preparation order for the command of the 28th Division and that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could the e-court show D52, which is a document created on the basis of this preparatory order, which is not the end of the story. Thank you, now we have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And in line 1 you see: "The soldiers of the 28th Ground Forces Division located in Srebrenica and Zepa," so this division is in Srebrenica, "although completely encircled and facing major problems relating to survival and the obligation to protect free territory, decided to contribute as much as possible to the fight against the aggressor ...," and so on and so on. Now the first bullet point says: "60 Chetniks were liquidated, and according to unconfirmed reports, the aggressor suffered even greater losses and had many wounded." Then they enumerate all the things that were burned, seised, and what livestock was stolen. And then it says: "In the village of Visnjica large quantities of ammunition were seised, but the soldiers were exhausted and could not remove it, so the ammunition was destroyed, as were all the facilities that the aggressor could use for military purposes." This was written on the 8th of July, 1995, at the command of the 28th Division of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they talk about the successes they have scored. Now, my question is: Was that preparatory order something that was followed up? Did it have certain consequences on the activities originating from the enclave, activities that you see referred to in the first line?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: As I told you, we have no information about military activities or preparations in what military form ever. So I did not know the existence of this order because one of the problems, of course, was that although one of my specialties was military security, the people from the BiH army had a very good military security and were very keen not telling what happened, so we were not aware of this. And, of course, again we face now in this document we can see now that 60 Chetniks were liquidated and all those kind of things. I only can refer to all the stories we heard when we were in the enclave speaking to either the Colonel Vukovic or Major Nikolic asking them to provide us with all the things we needed to do our job properly, I'm for sure that also the UNMOs asked several times to go with, for example, Major Nikolic outside the enclave to the spots where those kind of things happened and I don't deny that they might have happened, but we were never able to go there to check all those things. And of course, this is in a document of the Muslim Army when they stated that they have done this and seised all those material. Inside the enclave we don't have -- at least I didn't have the information that this was going on outside the enclave because we did not get those reports from our OPs, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Why then didn't you believe Vukovic and Nikolic and other Serbs when they were telling you that Muslims were launching activities from the protected area?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't say that we didn't believe them. Of course we believed them, but when we got to the point and wanted more information or wanted to check on the spot what happened, even where it exactly was, just to go there, even with an unarmed military observer who should have their freedom of movement to go out there and check all those stories they were telling us, we could do it for a big part inside the enclave because we were able to go there, but also in the enclave, they played the same game. We also had not in the whole enclave, the freedom of movement to go wherever we wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a moment ago that the Muslims had good security training, good security protection, or good security culture, whichever you call it, and they did not discuss their actions. Now, what else do you imply? What else do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I mean nothing else. The problem was that there was no standing army in the enclave. We had representatives from the Muslim Army who told us what they were, what their -- in some cases what their ranks were, but the way they acted at the moment we were there was not as a standing army. So we did not get any information about how their army was organised, and it was very difficult to get the information because they did no military training. We saw no military activities and they had no military headquarters or anything else. They were just representatives. And as you know, we had representatives, civilians and military, but at the end when the enclave fell, it was just mixed up and we saw that as well the civilians, as the military, all wore uniforms and had weapons, although we did our utmost to disarm them, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the statement made by Naser Oric that there were 4.000 rifles in Srebrenica during the withdrawal and the break-out of men from the Srebrenica enclave, of the Srebrenica troops from the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we get a citation to a statement of Mr. Oric on this point, or at least give us an idea of where you are getting it from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed that would be helpful for everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will provide a reference and the quotation tomorrow in e-court because it's a statement made by Naser Oric to the press after the fall of Srebrenica where he mentions both the break-out and the number of weapons. We'll find it tomorrow among the documents if we don't have to do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no problem with such a simple prospect as he heard such a statement, but I would like to know what the point of all this is. What is its relevance? I think at this point the General must know that the Prosecution actually has presented most of the guts of what he is talking about, the Muslim attacks and their policies and what was going on. It doesn't appear he is doing it for the credibility of this witness. So what really is the point? We have some six, seven-hour estimate here. I don't see any point to this. At some point time has to be compared to the point of the -- of what the Defence is doing, and I don't see the point. It's not contested. Fundamentally, these issues are not contested. In fact, they are, as we've stated, part of the adjudicated facts, part of the Prosecution's case. How many hours are we spending on non-contested issues that don't relate to the credibility of the witness on documents that this witness has never seen? At some point, if he could tell us, then I might be able to understand it, but I can't understand it at this point because he has not made any particular showing of what the point is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir, are you able to help us, the Chamber and the Prosecution and especially the witness about the position of Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. This witness denied any military activity originating from the demilitarised zone. I pointed out a part of his statement in which Colonel Vukovic told him about it, then I pointed out a passage where the Muslims themselves talked about these activities. I showed him a preparatory order made by their General Staff. He says it's just a preparatory order. I was trying to tell him that it's common knowledge among everyone, except perhaps the Dutch Battalion. I want to see if he knows or perhaps he justifies the activities of the Muslims and the lack of activity on the part of the Dutch Battalion, and I want to find out what the command of the Dutch Battalion thought about it because this witness was an advisor to the command of the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I appreciate that, but of course he is misstating the witness's testimony. The witness denied not that it happened, but denied having knowledge of it. Now, of course he can bring up these things to show it happened, but that is -- is he really challenging the credibility of the witness? If so, it's been challenged, how many more documents does he want to bring up on this point. There needs to be some limit because we are fighting the war all over again here and I think the point has been made, and if he is really going after his credibility like he says, let him do it. Do it. I have no problem with that. But let the witness know what he is doing as opposed to just having the witness read documents and quiz the witness on what is in the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed that was my understanding of the answers of the witness as well, that he denied having knowledge of these activities. This is indeed a difference to -- that he, as you said, that he denied these activities. This is indeed the difference. I think it's a good point in time for the second break and you should consider the objection of Mr. McCloskey, or indeed not the objection, but the request of Mr. McCloskey to focus on that what this witness can provide. We adjourn and resume ten minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. I hope you considered with your legal advisor during the break how to speed up the examination, and now please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will finish as we planned. It was necessary to ask those questions in order to present the witness with a view of the general situation in which the attack on enclave took place. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You spoke about the freedom of movement, that's where we left it off before the break. When it comes to the freedom of movement of the Dutch Battalion within the enclave, can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes. We had freedom of movement in the enclave until a certain moment and I don't know exactly when, one of our OPs was not manned and we tried to man it, the military people from the BiH in the enclave did not agree with the location of the OP because they thought they had much better places to put an OP over there in the western part of the enclave, and at a certain moment, they denied us access to a triangle in the western part of the enclave, so we had no freedom of movement over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you a member of the battalion when the movement or the freedom of movement was restricted, and can you remember the month when that happened?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I have to check in my notes, but I think it was in the beginning -- I think it was in February or March, just from my head now but I don't know the exact date now. But I can find it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need a date, we just need to know whether you were in Srebrenica when that happened, and if you say that that happened in March, that means that you were there; right?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I was there. I was in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You also said that in your statement. You stated that you arrived on the 4th or 5th of January, 1993. My next question is this --

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Maybe I can interrupt. I think there is a little mistake. I arrived on the 3rd of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, you arrived -- I must have misspoken. I'm reading from your statement where it says that you arrived on the 4th or 5th January, 1995, so I must have misspoken and we have to have a straight record. You arrived in 1995 and the events that you are describing for us happened later. Did you call the sector the Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you allowed to move within that Bandera Triangle? If not, could you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Well, I've got a problem to remind exactly why not. We were from the moment on that we had the problem over there with the Muslim army or the local Muslims over there, it wasn't really the army, it was the local Muslims over there denied us the access in the area. And I don't know exactly why it was. I know that we tried to create a new OP over there, the former OP-Bravo was over there, was removed. We wanted to create a new OP over there, and were not allowed to do it in the way we wanted it. After that we started patrolling in that triangle, in the Bandera Triangle, and also in the places where we tried to create a new OP, but in a certain moment, the access was denied and we had not the freedom of movement to go in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why were you not allowed access into that area?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I'm just looking in my notes, I don't know exactly what the reason was that we were not allowed to go in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While you are looking at your notes, could you please tell us whether you ever attended meetings which discussed the problem of the freedom of movement in the so-called Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, I have some information for you just after a quick look, here the 28th of February that we are trying -- we are talking about the Bandera Triangle with the UNMOs. The UNMOs were also not allowed to go into the Bandera Triangle, so that was at least in February that problem arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Will you allow me to jog your memory and maybe you will be able to provide us with some details.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce D66. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It is not my goal to contradict you. I am talking about some documents that you may not have seen and that's why I would like to show them to you. We can now see a document, or Exhibit D66, which was drafted by the BiH army. The document hails from the command of the 8th OG in Srebrenica and the date is 28th January, 1995. And the OG sent that to the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as to the command of the 2nd Corps. It was signed by Naser Oric. The document speaks about the situation in the sector of Podgaj village, as it was on the 9th of January, 1995, and the restriction of movement of the UNPROFOR forces in the wider region of Suceska and Podgaj. And in the second paragraph it says that there will be a restriction of movement in the area for UNPROFOR troops. Have I been able to jog your memory of the events?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we are talking about the same and I'm also looking in my notes. I have not read this specifically before, so it's just from my memory or I have to take some time and look in my diary or in my notes about those periods. Yeah, just from my memory, I can recall that indeed they wanted to speak, but that happened several times, with the commander of UNPROFOR. And from my memory, I think that even commander UNPROFOR visited the enclave and I don't know exactly when, and I also don't know if he spoke to Naser Oric at that moment. But that rings a bell, but I don't know exactly how or when.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you were the UNPROFOR liaison officer at the time, in January, that is?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: As stated in the beginning of the session, I had a double task. I was the responsible for the field security and advice commander of the Dutch Battalion on the field security. That was my main task. And after that, and parallel to that, I was the liaison officer. So all the time I played a double role being liaison officer, talking to civilian and military people and advising commander on the field security issues. So although you ask me a lot of questions up until now, I also have the impression that I was a kind of operation officer and know exactly all the military operations that were going on. Of course, I knew a lot of them, but some of the things I was not involved in, so also in my notes I've got not everything about what happened within the battalion, within the several companies in the area. And, of course, when you've got particular questions, I can try to check in my diary and in my notebooks if I got information about it, but you have to be a little bit specific and tell me what you want to know so I can check because I provided the -- Mr. McCloskey with big parts of my diary and from my notebooks, but I don't think that we went back until February with the copying of the notebooks. And if you're interested, it's no problem for me to make a copy and provide you with the information. At this moment, maybe you can feel from my answers, I've got a problem, I have facts that are in my notes and in my diary, and I've got memories, and the problem is that now and then I've got a memory who don't fits into my notebooks and I think the notebook should be leading because those are the facts, and in 15 years' time memories change.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for the offer, we will be grateful to have it. The document that is before you, could you please look at its second paragraph or rather, the third line in that paragraph. It says here: "The commander of the 281st Eastern Bosnia Light Brigade, in co-operation with the commander of the 2nd Corps after a warning that UNPROFOR troops should not move within a certain area, has enclosed the area." That's from lines 3 to 5. Are you the liaison officer which is mentioned here as having reached an agreement with the commander of the 281st Brigade? Are you that liaison officer? Were you that liaison officer or not?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't even know the existence of the 281st Eastern Bosnian Light Brigade. The only people we dealed with were from the 8th Operational Group which was called later on, I think, the 28th Operational Group and not specifically the 281st Light Brigade. There were several commanders in that part and I think that in that area one of the commanders was Zuzo Tuzanovic [phoen]. I don't know exactly what area his responsibility was but when we are talking about the Bandera Triangle, I think that Zuzo Tuzanovic was responsible over there. And I never dealed with him because he was not available for us to do business with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you meet with any officer, if you did not meet with the commander, as you say, in respect of the problems that arose in this sector of Suceska and Podgaj villages, and did you take any positions with regard to that situation?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, as I remember now, the only officers we dealed with were Naser Oric and his second in command, Ramiz, at that time, and not with the other commanders in the field. Most of the time, the company commanders from the Bravo Company and the Charlie Company, the Bravo Company was stationed in Srebrenica town and the Charlie Company was stationed in the compound in Potocari, they also had divided the whole enclave. And I don't know if commander of the Bravo Company or the commander of the Charlie Company maybe dealed with this commanders. I really don't know. The only people we dealed with were the top of the HOG.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with those men from the top echelons of the Srebrenica enclave command to discuss the problems that we are talking about right now, and that's the restriction of movement in the sector of Suceska and Podgaj?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: In my memory, we talk about this with Naser Oric and with Ramiz, his second in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what was it that you discussed with Naser Oric and his second in command, Ramiz?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I have to do this from my memory because I don't have the facts so at this moment. But of course, we tried to get the freedom of movement again in that area and they denied so that was a problem. And as we dealed with the VRS who did not allow UNPROFOR to do what he had to do, it was the same with the Bosnians, the Bosnian army in the enclave in this case, in the Bandera Triangle. And I think, but that's also just from my memory, that commander DutchBat didn't want to create a big problem in the enclave because we also had a lack of everything, so not a possibility to go in there in a military way and just take over the area. Not only because we had no -- not the means, but also not the personnel to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And when it comes to the agreement, were representatives of the Army of the Republika Srpska duty-bound to ensure your unrestricted movement wherever you wanted in their territory at your request?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think the agreement for the freedom of movement from the VRS was very clear. It started for me on the 3rd of January when we went into the enclave. We were not free as UNPROFOR to go freely into the enclave, to take over from our predecessors the enclave, and just go and do our job over there. We had to stop on several check-points. We were checked and were not allowed to bring in all the things we needed. It was already seen with the 1st and 2nd Battalion that they were not allowed to bring in all the ammunition and all the other things they needed in the enclave, so that part of the freedom of movement was not there at all. And that stayed all the time because we were not allowed to act outside of the enclave, out of the red line as we drew it on the map, because the VRS did not agree that we went out of the enclave to go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you are drawing a parallel between the freedom of movement within the Bandera Triangle and the freedom of movement across the entire Republika Srpska, could you tell us, is the Republika Srpska to be blamed for your restricted movement in the area known as Bandera Triangle that you were supposed to supervise according to the agreement?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think we are getting now to a political part of the whole story. When you send as UN a battalion to a certain area, I think as UN you have the responsibility to arrange that they go in there as a battalion being able to do a military job if needed. If you accept from in this case the VRS, that you sent in a battalion partly demilitarised, having not enough weapons, having not enough ammunition, having not enough other logistic means to do the job in a proper way, then I think we should blame the UN, and of course the VRS did it in their way but had a possibility to do it in their way. And that's of course the same for the Muslims in the enclave because when you don't have, for example, enough diesel to travel around in your vehicles, then you give them the possibility to play with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now could you please answer the following question: Why were you not allowed to move around in the Bandera Triangle, although you had every right to do so according to the agreement? Do you know it now and did you know it at the time when the ban was imposed?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, I have to take a look in my notes. I can't scan them now as quick as I would like, but I can't give you an answer right now. And I don't know if it's in my notes because it's an operational question and I should find something from one of the meetings with the leaders of operational group, but I can't find it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe you can tell us tomorrow when you find the notes. And now, please tell me this: The restriction of movement in the so-called Bandera Triangle, was that imposed upon you because the Muslims were preparing to join up the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica of the sort described in the document that I had showed you just awhile ago?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Again, I have to do it from my mind now and seeing the map in my mind. The Bandera Triangle was in the middle of the enclave. So in the southern part we were able to patrol and to be in our OPs and when you want to connect Zepa and Srebrenica, then it should be the southern part that you deny UNPROFOR the access and not in the middle of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you whether that was one of the reasons, and I pointed to it in document D52 where it says literally joining up the enclaves. And in that document, Rasim Delic reports to Alija Izetbegovic about the joining up of the enclaves. Was that a possible reason or one of the possible reasons? You will remember that that is a document I was reading from just before the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have the document on the screen, if he is going to be asking specific questions about it so the witness can have a chance to review it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The document was displayed just a minute ago and that's one of the bullet points that I wanted the witness to read. And in that bullet point Mr. Delic reported to Alija Izetbegovic about what had been done with helicopter sorties and then you protested because I was showing the document. Can we again see D67, the document which talks about helicopter sorties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I must confess that I'm confused now. You were first referring to the document D52, then Mr. McCloskey asked that we can see that and now you are referring to another, D67. What are you talking about, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm talking about D67. I may have switched the numbers in my previous request. Can we please look at D67 again, page 1, bullet point 4. Thank you. And in English it's on page 2, bullet point 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's not waste time, I'll read from bullet point 4 in the Serbian and you should look at bullet point 2: "In preparations for a future operation to link up the enclaves, we brought in and took back four brigade commanders, two brigade Chiefs of Staff, and the 26th Division Chief of Staff. The division commander who was meant to go on the next helicopter flight did not return. After the final flight ended tragically, Naser remained." You said that for awhile Naser was not in the enclave, that he was replaced by Becirovic. Does this document speak about the linking up of the enclaves, and was your restriction of movement in the Bandera Triangle perhaps related to the process to link up the enclaves, or the preparations to do so? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I'm now acting on the strategic level from the BiH command, I think. Of course, there might be a possibility, but from my point of view, the Bandera Triangle was in the middle of the enclave, from the middle of the enclave going a little bit to the west and then opens up as a triangle. The only direction I can face in this case is the direction of Sarajevo, but there is so many territory between the western part of the enclave and Sarajevo that is for me no logical explanation that this should be a link to another enclave and especially not to Zepa because Zepa was in the southern part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see D65. Can this be blown up and can the blown-up version be shown to the witness, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see the triangle with numbers 1, 2, and then a letter X and then arrow?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that perhaps the area where it was forbidden to you to move around?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: In my first opinion I say, yes, this is the area. This is the Bandera Triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it in the centre or on the outskirts of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: You see the smallest part of the triangle is in the middle of the enclave and then it's going westwards and opens because I can't see exactly. But I think that the red line is the enclave -- is marking enclave, maybe the black line, I don't know exactly, but from the middle of the enclave westwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The black line denotes parties to the conflict. The red line also and in between them is the interval, the no-man's land. Does that mean anything to you? Were you able to move within this triangle, you, the UN force?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think you explain now that there's a red line and a black line and no-man's land in between. What I can recall in my memory is that we only had one red line that was a circle around the enclave and there was no space and no doubt about it. And of course, Muslims and Serbs were angry and about where the line should be and which tree was Serb or Muslim tree, but we never used a map like this. And as I stated, the blue triangle, as you can see it over there, is, in my opinion, so the Bandera Triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your tenure in Srebrenica from January to July 1995, was the UNPROFOR allowed to move within this blue triangle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That has been asked and answered several times. I would also like to know the relevance at this point. The Bandera Triangle and the fact that UNPROFOR did not have movement there is not a contested issue. That the Muslims intended to join the enclaves is not a contested issue. These don't appear to be going to credibility. Can we have some idea of where this is going? What the relevance of this is? I still don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I can respond. We are talking about the reasons for the attack against the enclave and we are still going in circles about the questions I asked and never got an answer to. And I'm asking again, who approved for the Muslims to set up complete control over the Bandera Triangle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think this is not correct. The witness answered several times that the UNPROFOR had no access to this triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- it would be helpful but one of stated reasons in the attack plan of the Serbs to attack Srebrenica was to separate the two enclaves, Zepa and Srebrenica. It's the position of the Prosecution that that was a legitimate concern and a legitimate objective of the VRS because of the -- what was going on inside the enclaves. We agree with that. That is a part of our case. That's part of our expert report. So I agree with -- if that's Mr. Tolimir is trying to justify that part of the attack, I agree that that was legitimate. But when there are more than one reasons for an attack and other reasons are illegitimate, that is the part we are focusing on and that was the -- our position that the attack was also to remove the civilian population which is a crime. But I agree that General Tolimir, if that's what he is trying to do, that the Muslims caused trouble, as this witness has talked about, and one of the reasons for the attack was to stop that trouble. We agree with that. That's part of our case. It's in our reports. If that's where he is going, maybe we can save some time. But it's his case, but it's nice to know that is where he going because he just said that, but for whatever it's worth that's the Prosecution's position on that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I refer you to page 76, line 11 and 12, and again you asked, I quote: "In your tenure in Srebrenica from January to July 11, 1995 was the UNPROFOR allowed to move within this blue triangle." And this was the trigger of the concern of Mr. McCloskey and we've received a lot of information from this witness. Please use your time of cross-examination in the best way and carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I would like correction to the record. I asked: Do you know whether it is the case that from January until July 1995 the UNPROFOR was not allowed to move within the Bandera Triangle. Perhaps it was not interpreted fully or accurately because we were speaking very fast and that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's exactly the same formulation of the question again. And the witness said they had no access to that triangle. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not ask a question. I just said the transcript needed to be corrected. What I said was from January to July, not just July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is exactly what is recorded. Indeed I see now on page 78, line 3, this is the wrong quotation of your words in July 11, 1995. There must be a mistake, but carry on, I think we all know what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, be so kind as to tell us, the activities that the BH army carried out in the area called the Bandera Triangle, were they known or unknown to the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: As you know, from the moment on the Bandera Triangle existed we were not allowed to go in, and I can't recall at this moment and I have no all the reports, of course, if we discovered any military activity and if we acted against it. I think I can state that if we saw any military activity in the enclave, I would have known it and I would have brought it up in a meeting with Ramiz or with Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In another answer you said the UNPROFOR commander dealt with the Bandera Triangle problem. Can you tell us how exactly he dealt with it and what orders were you given as a result?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, I don't know exactly at this moment. It's just I'm still looking in my diary what exactly happened and what was the reason of the existence of the Bandera Triangle. And I also don't know what the orders of the commander DutchBat were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it true that you said a moment ago that it was the UNPROFOR commander who dealt with and resolved this, or did I mishear you?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I think when we are talking about the UNPROFOR commander, I think I'm talking about commander DutchBat because that was the commander I'm talking about all the time. I had no connections or information --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have information whatsoever about so-called Carter Agreement?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: It doesn't ring a bell at this moment. What do you mean with the Carter Agreement and what information should I have about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Some of the information available to military observers who are present at the meetings where the problem of the Bandera Triangle was dealt with, there are entries referring to the Carter Agreement. You can look it up tomorrow and you can answer tomorrow, if you wish, because you say you are not prepared to do so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you should help the witness and explain why -- what do you mean by Carter Agreement. The witness doesn't know that and you should put the question in an appropriate way to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you want to answer now, then tell us if you know anything, anything at all about the Carter Agreement that has to do with Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness answered this question already with a word: "It doesn't ring a bell at this moment. What do you mean with the Carter Agreement and what information should I have about it." That was page 79, line 23 and 4. He asked you to explain what do you mean by the Carter Agreement. You should help him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I explained that one of the participants in the meetings where this was discussed said that a decision had been made in keeping with the Carter Agreement, and I asked this question without meaning any offence or without meaning to test your credibility, but you were present at the meetings where the UNPROFOR commander dealt with this issue. If you don't know, then we can move on. I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: I don't know at this moment. As I said, it doesn't ring a bell and I don't have information about a meeting at this moment where the Carter Agreement was discussed or referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think then, indeed, you should move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether the DutchBat had information that there would be an attack against the enclave?

utterances.speaker: EVERT RAVE
utterances.text: No, we had not the information that an attack was planned against the enclave. But planning on this session, I read my diaries from I think April or May up until July, and what I analyse now is seeing what happened in whole Bosnia, seeing what was happening in and around the enclave, it's amazing that we didn't see it before and not only we, because we were only a part of the whole thing, of course, we sent our information to north-east command and from there to BH command. I think that from my point of view when we get all the information that we face now and when I see if from my diaries, what I write and the information what I get is that it was clear from me that it is not strange that an attack should take place. But we had not specific information that an attack would take place on the enclave. Of course, we got several signs that commanders told us and that started on the 3rd or 6th of January, where General Zivanovic told us that the enclave of Srebrenica was his, at least the southern part of the enclave was his, not from Mladic, not from Karadzic, not from anybody but it was his. So on the 6th of January, in my opinion, he announced already that he wanted back his part of the enclave. And I think that was one of the things that was in our mind when finally the enclave -- when indeed the attack on the enclave started, the words of the General Zivanovic, which we thought of course was responsible for the attack because it was in his area of responsibility in our point of view, that he would take the southern part of the enclave because it was his enclave or his territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to adjourn now. We just passed 7.00 and we will resume tomorrow in the morning at 9.00 in this courtroom. Please be reminded that you are no allowed to have contact about the content of your evidence to either party. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get an estimate of the remaining cross just for everyone's planning purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I've stressed already, we will finish within the time we were given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The time you have given, you have given, six hours. But after the experience of today, perhaps you can indicate if it is possible to finish during the first session of tomorrow's hearing or at a later stage, that will be really helpful for the Chamber and for the parties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We announced six to seven hours and I don't think we have used up that time, and we cannot use it up even if we continue the whole day tomorrow. I will do my best to finish tomorrow, if that is helpful to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we don't receive any indication today. We will see what happens tomorrow. We adjourn and resume tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of October, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
